h1: Your agency wants more money mid-contract: three legitimate reasons and two that are not
metaTitle: SEO Agency Wants to Raise the Retainer?
metaDescription: Three reasons that justify a re-quote and two that do not, plus the quieter version: same price, fewer deliverables. What to ask before you agree.
answer: Three things justify a mid-contract increase: the site materially grew, a channel was added, or a pass-through cost moved and the agency isn't absorbing it. Two don't: they under-priced the pitch, or they've realised you now depend on them. Ask to see the evidence before you argue about the number.
takeaways: A price rise is a **proposal to change the deal**, not an announcement. You are allowed to say no and keep the original terms until they run out.
Legitimate triggers come with evidence attached. "Costs have gone up" without a document is a mispriced pitch being corrected at your expense.
The quieter version is **same price, fewer deliverables**. Check the current month against the original scope, not against last month.
Counter with a scope change rather than a price change. If the work genuinely grew, something else can shrink.

sections.h2: The three reasons that hold up
body: Agencies do sometimes have a real case. It's rarer than the emails suggest, and it always comes with something you can look at.

The first is that the site materially grew. A 300-URL brochure site and a 6,000-URL catalogue are different jobs — more templates to keep clean, more internal linking to maintain, more ways for indexing to go wrong. Google's own guidance is blunt about where scale starts to bite: crawl budget only becomes a live concern for [sites past a million pages, or ten thousand pages that change daily](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/large-site-managing-crawl-budget). Below that, "your site got bigger" justifies more money when it means more pages to write and maintain — not because crawling suddenly became hard.

The second is that a channel was added. If SEO quietly grew to include managing your Google Ads account, that's a second discipline and a second fee, and it should have been quoted as one before the work started.

The third is that a pass-through cost moved and the agency isn't willing to absorb it. Media spend, a licence billed at cost, a tax change. This one should never arrive as a fee increase — it should arrive as a line item with a document behind it. Rising click costs don't count, incidentally: an auction sets those, competitiveness moves them, and they'd have moved the same way under any agency.

body: The first is that they mispriced the pitch. This is the most common one and it's almost never said out loud, because the honest sentence — "we quoted low to win you and it isn't profitable" — is hard to type. It shows up instead as vague talk of rising costs, more competitive markets, or the account needing more attention than expected.

It's worth some sympathy and no money. An agency that under-quoted made a commercial judgement and got it wrong. Passing that error to you halfway through is asking you to pay for their sales strategy. Where it becomes a genuine red flag is when the same agency is still quoting low to new prospects — then it isn't a mistake, it's a model.

The second is repricing because you now depend on them. It has a signature: the increase arrives after a good quarter, or right after a migration only they understand, or at the exact moment your in-house marketer leaves. Nothing about the work has changed. What's changed is the cost to you of saying no. That cost is real — we've written it up in [the real cost of switching SEO agencies](/journal/the-real-cost-of-switching-seo-agencies) — and an agency that prices against it has stopped selling you work and started selling you back your own switching cost.

Both versions often arrive wrapped in a promise: a bigger fee to "finally get you to position one". Nobody can promise that position — Google's own guidance for hiring an SEO says as much — and a commitment that can't be kept isn't a reason to pay more. A promise against your own baseline, with a number and a date attached, is a different thing entirely.

callout.title: The timing tell
callout.body: Ask yourself what changed in the fortnight before the email. If the answer is "we renewed", "we passed the point where leaving would hurt", or "our internal person left", the increase is about your position, not the work. Legitimate triggers arrive when the work changes, which is almost never the same week as your renewal.

sections.h2: The quieter version: same price, fewer deliverables
body: Most retainers don't get more expensive. They get thinner, which is the same thing with better manners.

It happens gradually enough to be invisible month to month. Four articles becomes three, then three shorter ones. The monthly technical sweep becomes a quarterly one. The named strategist becomes a coordinator forwarding a deck. Every individual month looks like the one before it — that's the trick. You have to compare against the original scope document, not against last month.

So go and find it. If you can't, that's the finding: nobody wrote down what you were buying, which means nobody can prove it shrank. [What should be in an SEO contract](/answers/what-should-be-in-an-seo-contract) covers what the document needs to contain to be worth having.
numbered: Pull the original scope or proposal. List every deliverable with its promised frequency.
Tick off what actually shipped in the last three months. Use dates, not impressions — publish dates, ticket dates, report dates.
Count the named people. If the strategist you were sold hasn't been on a call in two months, the seniority you're paying for has quietly left the account.
Send the comparison, not the complaint. "The scope says four articles a month; we had seven in the last quarter" is a conversation. "I don't feel we're getting value" is a negotiation you'll lose.

sections.h2: Counter with a scope change, not a price change
body: If the work genuinely grew, the money isn't the only variable. Something else can shrink.

That reframes the conversation from "do I pay 30% more" to "what does 30% more work look like, and is it work I want". Often it isn't. An agency that needs another ₹25,000 a month to maintain 4,000 new URLs may be maintaining pages that should be consolidated or removed — in which case the right answer is a smaller site, not a larger invoice.
Four counters worth having in your pocket.
bullets: **Hold the price, change the mix.** Drop two articles a month, add the technical maintenance the growth actually created.
**Stage it.** Agree the increase from the quarter after next, conditional on the same numbers you're already measuring. If they won't tie it to the metric, they don't believe it either.

**Buy the new thing at list price.** If a channel was added, pay the published price for that channel and keep the original retainer untouched. Bundled increases are how two separate decisions become one you can't examine.

**Ask for the sunset.** If the trigger was a migration or a one-off catalogue expansion, the extra fee should end when the extra work does. Put the end date in writing now, because nobody has ever volunteered it later.

callout.title: You can also just say no
callout.body: A mid-contract increase is a proposal to vary an agreement you both signed. Until you accept it, the original terms stand for whatever remains of the term. Saying "no, let's revisit at renewal" is a complete answer, and an agency that treats it as a crisis has told you how much they need your money — which is useful information whichever way you decide.

sections.h2: What would make us re-quote, published so you can hold us to it
body: We publish fixed prices — SEO from ₹75,000/mo, smaller sites from ₹40,000, organic social at ₹30,000, ₹50,000 or ₹70,000, performance at ₹40,000, ₹75,000 or ₹1,50,000, and the bundles at ₹99,000 and ₹1,75,000. A published price is only worth something if the conditions for changing it are published too.
So here they are. This is a commitment you can quote back at us, which is the only kind worth making.

Yes. New scope, quoted from the same published list — a band change, not a percentage.

No. Our performance fee is a fixed monthly number, not a percentage of your media.

No. We took that risk when we published a price.

No. Being useful is not a reason to charge more for the same work.
GST changes
Not a fee change. The tax line moves and the fee doesn't — see [GST on digital marketing services](/cost/gst-on-digital-marketing-services).

sections.h2: When the right answer is to leave anyway
body: Sometimes the increase is fine and the relationship isn't. A 20% rise on work you can't evaluate is 20% more of a problem you already had.

The test we'd apply: if the fee were going down 20% instead, would you renew? If the answer is still no, price was never the issue and negotiating it just buys you another two quarters of the same reporting.

Before you decide either way, get the baseline straight — what you were measuring, what it was on day one, and where it is now. If nobody can produce that, the increase is unanswerable in both directions. [Can I fire my SEO agency](/answers/can-i-fire-my-seo-agency) covers the exit mechanics, and [how to split a marketing budget](/cost/marketing-budget-split-between-seo-paid-and-social) is worth reading first if the honest answer is that the money should go somewhere else entirely.

Our own terms exist partly to make this conversation cheap: month to month after the first quarter, thirty days' notice, and you keep every asset. An agency that has to be difficult about leaving has already told you what its renewals are built on.

faqs.q: Is a mid-contract price increase normal for a marketing agency?
faqs.a: Increases at renewal are normal. Increases mid-term are not, unless the scope changed. If the deliverables in your contract are unchanged and the fee is being raised, you're being asked to fund a mispriced pitch or your own dependency, not extra work.

faqs.q: What evidence should an agency show before raising the retainer?
faqs.a: Something you can look at. A crawl export showing the site grew, a scope document for a channel that was added, or a vendor invoice for a pass-through cost. "Our costs have gone up" with nothing attached is a statement about their business, not about your account.

faqs.q: My agency kept the price but reduced the deliverables. Is that allowed?
faqs.a: Not if the scope specified frequencies. Pull the original document, tick off what actually shipped over the last three months with dates, and send the comparison. Silent scope reduction is a price increase per unit of work, and it's much easier to reverse than a stated one.

faqs.q: How do I renegotiate an SEO retainer without losing the relationship?
faqs.a: Negotiate scope rather than price. Ask what the extra money buys, then ask what could come out to fund it. Offer to stage the increase from the following quarter tied to a metric you already track. Agencies that believe their own case accept that; agencies that don't, won't.

faqs.q: Can I refuse and keep the current price?
faqs.a: For the remainder of the term, generally yes — an increase is a proposal to vary the agreement, not a notice. Read your notice period and auto-renewal clause first, then say you'd rather revisit at renewal. How they react tells you more than the number did.

faqs.q: Should the fee go up when I increase my ad spend?
faqs.a: Not automatically, and we'd argue not at all. A percentage-of-spend fee pays the agency more for spending more of your money, which is a bad incentive dressed as a fair one. A fixed monthly management fee keeps that decision yours.
